hypothesis: The baseline’s r-c-k order reads B with a stride. Blocking row, column, and reduction ranges while using i-k-j within each tile should make B and C accesses contiguous and keep a small output tile local. The k tiles advance in order, preserving each output element’s increasing-k accumulation sequence. A 32-by-32 tile is a generic cache-locality hypothesis, not a hardware-specific guarantee.

The baseline's row/column/reduction order walks B with a stride and does not expose a SIMD-friendly output loop. A 4x8 outer-product tile should reuse four A values across eight output columns, reuse each contiguous B segment across four rows, and keep 32 partial sums local; the SIMD column loop may improve arithmetic throughput. Scalar dot products cover row and column tails. The baseline is correct and measured at 0.1339 s mean over three samples (baseline-e1), but there is no candidate measurement or size-specific breakdown, so this is a testable hypothesis rather than a claimed speedup.

Static OpenMP scheduling across disjoint output rows should reduce compute time for large matrices at four threads, while retaining the existing accumulation order. A single serial memset and one parallel loop keep output initialization and OpenMP region costs inside the run; one-thread and four-thread timings can test whether compute savings offset those costs. No speedup is assumed before measurement.

This is a materially different control from the recent 32-by-32-by-32 blocked i-k-j kernel: it removes all blocking and packing, changing only the loop order from r-c-k to scalar i-k-j. Contiguous B and C accesses may retain most of the tiled kernel's benefit; without tiles, repeated B traversal and the active C row may instead hurt larger sizes. Repeated complete-call timings, including memset, should distinguish these possibilities. Reject the control if it is incorrect or at least 10% slower than the blocked candidate in every matched large-size configuration; retaining comparable timings would support loop interchange as the primary locality benefit, not prove it.

The measured 4x8 candidate used one sequential accumulation chain per output. This base-derived experiment keeps its 4x8 spatial tile and SIMD column loop, but splits each reduction into even- and odd-k accumulator banks so independent chains may hide multiply-accumulate latency. That trades extra live accumulators and a final sum for instruction-level parallelism; register spills or altered rounding may erase the benefit. Test correctness on arbitrary sizes and tails, then compare target-build timings on the analyst-suggested n=384 and n=768 cases against both the base and measured 4x8 reference. Stop if correctness fails or if the split-k version does not improve large-case time over the 4x8 reference without a material regression elsewhere.

The selected parent enters an OpenMP parallel-for region even when the bounded team size is one. Use the same row arithmetic and accumulation order in both paths, but execute the row loop directly when team_size==1; retain static OpenMP scheduling for larger teams. This may lower full-call 1-thread time at larger sizes without changing the four-thread path. The hypothesis is falsified if repeated 1-thread medians do not improve at both n=384 and n=768, if the 4-thread path repeatedly regresses, or if correctness fails.

The two distinct valid T3 programs have close overall means (0.066445 s and 0.066636 s); prior per-size observations show strong four-thread row-parallel performance but little one-thread change, and both approaches retain a separate memset. This experiment tests a different mechanism: initialize a local accumulator for each output and store it once, eliminating the separate serial clear while keeping the same increasing-k row kernel for direct serial and static OpenMP execution. Repeated full-call 1- and 4-thread measurements at n=384 and n=768 should show whether removing the clear improves end-to-end time; initialization and OpenMP costs remain inside the timed call. The hypothesis is falsified if correctness fails or repeated measurements show no improvement at both sizes and thread counts, or a repeatable four-thread regression.

The two distinct measured programs in the catalog were both correct; the scalar i-k-j candidate had a lower mean time (0.01043 s) than the three-axis 32-tile candidate (0.03855 s). This experiment tests a different mechanism: i-j-panel-k-j ordering with a 64-column panel may keep a smaller C region active across the full increasing-k accumulation while preserving contiguous accesses within each B/C segment. It could help for large rows, but rereads A across panels and may impair B streaming or add loop overhead. Expected observation: any locality benefit should appear in repeated large-size complete-call timings, not correctness alone. Stop pursuing it if incorrect, if repeated n=768 timings show less than 5% improvement over scalar i-k-j, or if n=384 regresses by more than 5%; a promising result still needs confirmation.

Earlier valid attempts tested static row computation with serial clearing, a direct serial branch, or eliminating the clear with per-output accumulators. This experiment instead tests row-parallel output initialization followed by the same increasing-k row kernel inside one bounded OpenMP team. At four threads, distributing initialization may reduce full-call time for larger matrices; at one thread, the shared arithmetic helper takes a direct serial path. This is falsified if full-call 4-thread timings at n=384 and n=768 do not improve against the relevant row-parallel reference, if timings regress repeatedly, or if correctness fails. Initialization and OpenMP costs must remain in the timed calls.

The measured 4×8 variants are both correct, with the split-k candidate fastest (6eb0414411374db4: 0.004785 s mean; 7d1ad999b6a2442a: 0.005681 s). The target-build test should compare against the measured 4×8 reference on n=384 and 768, and exercise tails at n=385; check correctness on all valid sizes, including signed inputs. Stop if correctness fails or the 4×16 kernel does not improve large-size timings over split-k 4×8 without a material regression elsewhere. No speedup is claimed before measurement.

The measured scalar i-k-j candidate (6e527b906ff34591, mean 0.01043 s) was faster than both the 32-cube blocked candidate (5100c500e2af480a, 0.03855 s) and the 64-column-panel candidate (859e7e99997544fe, 0.02275 s). Expected observation: if panel overhead mattered, repeated n=768 timings should move toward the scalar result; otherwise the panel may remain slower or regress. Stop if incorrect, if it fails to improve at least 5% over scalar at n=768, or if it regresses over 5% at n=384.

The recent valid variants use OpenMP worksharing (`parallel for schedule(static)`) for row assignment, and their overall means are close (0.0664–0.0672 s). This candidate tests a distinct scheduling mechanism: manually divide rows into balanced contiguous ranges using the actual team size, while retaining the same increasing-k row kernel and one in-call output clear. This may reduce worksharing dispatch overhead at four threads. Compare full-call 1- and 4-thread results, including initialization and OpenMP costs, at n=384 and n=768. The hypothesis is falsified if repeated four-thread measurements show no improvement over the static-worksharing reference, show a regression, or correctness fails; no speedup is assumed.

A per-call, cache-tiled transpose of B may trade allocation and packing cost for contiguous B-column loads in increasing-k dot products, while keeping A rows contiguous and writing every C element. This differs from the measured scalar i-k-j and output-panel loops. Repeated complete-call timings at large and small sizes can falsify the idea: if packing-inclusive times do not improve on scalar i-k-j at large n, or regress materially at smaller n, the packing cost/locality trade is unfavorable. No speedup is assumed.

Test a generic 8×8 outer-product tile against the measured 4×16 and 4×8 kernels. For the same 64 outputs per k, the 8×8 shape loads eight A and eight B values rather than four A and sixteen B values for the 4×16 shape, potentially balancing reuse while keeping the contiguous eight-column loop SIMD-friendly. The larger row block or compiler register allocation could instead hurt. The expected observation is lower target-build time on n=384 and 768 if balanced reuse helps; n=385 exercises row/column tails and an odd reduction length. Stop if correctness fails or if repeated target timings do not beat the 4×16 reference on large cases without material regressions; make no speedup claim before measurement.

Test a 2×16 outer-product microkernel with a single sequential k-accumulation chain. Unlike the recent 4×8, 4×16, 8×8, and split-k variants, it keeps the 16-column SIMD-friendly loop but halves the live tile accumulators versus 4×16 (32 rather than 64 floats). If register pressure in the larger tile limits target code generation, this may reduce large-size time; if reuse is more important or 4×16 already fits well, it may be slower. Compare repeated single-thread target-build timings at n=384 and 768, and validate tails at n=385. Stop on any correctness failure or if it does not give a repeatable large-size improvement without a material regression; no speedup is claimed before measurement.

The five distinct valid T3 programs have closely clustered overall means (about 0.0664–0.0672 s), and recent approaches primarily assigned whole rows or contiguous row ranges. Tiling may alter work distribution and locality, but could also add overhead; compare full-call 1- and 4-thread results at n=384 and 768, with the single memset included, and treat no repeatable improvement or a correctness failure as falsifying the hypothesis.

The measured scalar i-k-j candidate (6e527b906ff34591) is faster than prior three-axis blocking and single-row column panels. Repeated complete-call timings can falsify the idea if it fails to improve over scalar i-k-j at large n or regresses at smaller sizes; no speedup is assumed.

Test four-step unrolling of the reduction loop in a 4×16 outer-product kernel. Unlike the recent tile-shape variants and even/odd split-k kernel, this retains one sequential accumulation chain per output and changes the k-loop mechanism: fewer loop-control steps may help while contiguous columns remain SIMD-vectorizable. Compare repeated target-build timings with the measured 4×16 variant (586558af72254ce8) at n=384 and 768; validate correctness and tails at n=385. The unrolled kernel may instead increase instruction pressure or be no faster; no speedup is claimed before measurement.

Prior valid variants used static rows, manual row ranges, or tiles; the row-oriented aggregate means for 3a55555c5c2247ab and 689a71f7808d4ce6 were close (about 0.0664–0.0665 s), while 66d33d5662484b94 used tiles. The base uses r-c-k order, which reads B with a stride; measured scalar i-k-j and 4-row-by-256-column tiling have close overall means (0.010431 s and 0.010379 s). This tests a different locality tradeoff: block four output rows across the full column range, reusing each contiguous B row across those rows without j-panel passes or repeated A traversal per panel. It may help if that B reuse outweighs the larger active C region; repeated complete-call timings, including memset, at small and large sizes can falsify the hypothesis. No speedup is assumed.

The measured candidates mostly use register-resident spatial tiles with different shapes, split-k accumulators, or reduction unrolling. This experiment instead tests an i-k-column update: each output row is initialized once and kept hot while the inner SIMD-friendly loop updates its contiguous columns from a contiguous B row. That should remove the baseline's strided B traversal, but repeatedly reading and writing C across k may outweigh the locality and vectorization benefit. Compare repeated target-build single-thread timings at n=384 and 768 against measured 4×16 candidate 586558af72254ce8; validate correctness at n=385 and across the controller's cases. The hypothesis is falsified if it is not consistently faster without a material regression; no speedup is assumed.

The measured four-row kernel that spans all columns averaged 0.009685 s, while a four-row-by-256-column tile averaged 0.010379 s and scalar i-k-j averaged 0.010431 s. This serial four-row-by-64-column tile tests whether a smaller active C region improves locality enough to offset rescanning panels and reloading A; all timings must include output initialization. Expect a benefit only if C residency is limiting. Stop pursuing it if repeated n=768 timings improve by less than 5%, regress by more than 5% at n=384, or correctness/complete-overwrite validation fails.

The visible measured candidates favor a 4×16 tile (0.003388 s mean) over tested 8×8 and 2×16 shapes, but those kernels rely on compiler lowering of a SIMD loop. This experiment keeps that tile and instead explicitly uses guarded AVX2 loads, broadcasts, and vector accumulators, with FMA when enabled. The compile-time guard leaves a portable SIMD-loop fallback when AVX2 is not enabled by the target build. It may be no faster than compiler-generated SIMD; no speedup is assumed. The hypothesis is tested by checking which path the target build takes, validating arbitrary tails and signed inputs, and comparing repeated timings at n=384 and 768 against the measured 4×16 candidate.

The selected parent 41ad initializes rows in a bounded OpenMP team, then uses a second static omp-for for computation. Retain that initialization, arithmetic helper, and serial path, but replace only the compute omp-for with balanced contiguous ranges computed from each thread's actual team rank and size. Expect any benefit only in full-call 4-thread timings at n=384 and 768; the 1-thread path should be unchanged. The measured four-row/full-width candidate averaged 0.009685 s, the four-row-by-256-column candidate 0.010379 s, and the four-row-by-64-column candidate 0.013599 s. This untested four-row-by-128-column tile tests whether an intermediate C-panel footprint retains four-row B reuse while reducing the active output region. If panel size is the relevant tradeoff, expect a benefit over the 256-column tile at n=768 without a greater than 5% regression against the full-width control at n=384. Stop if repeated complete-call timings, including memset, fail to improve at least 5% at n=768 or regress over 5% at n=384; correctness or complete-overwrite failure stops the experiment immediately.

Earlier measurements found the four-row/full-width kernel at 0.009685 s, scalar i-k-j at 0.010431 s, and whole-matrix B-transpose packing at 0.116563 s. This experiment tests a materially different, bounded packing mechanism: transpose only 32-by-64 B micro-panels into an 8 KiB per-call scratch buffer, then accumulate each output's k contributions in order using contiguous A and packed-B segments. The smaller scratch footprint may improve dot-product locality without the whole-matrix packing cost, but repeated panel packing, scalar reductions, and allocation may erase that benefit. Compare repeated complete-call timings, including output initialization, allocation, packing, and free; the hypothesis is unsupported if n=768 does not improve at least 5% over the scalar i-k-j control or n=384 regresses by more than 5%. Tail tiles and complete C overwrite must remain correct.

Refine selected parent 74d461538cab413b by retaining its 32-by-64 per-call B-panel scratch, packing, allocation and full output initialization, but store packed tiles in k-major order and use contiguous-j updates across up to four output rows instead of a scalar k-reduction for each output.
